newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Pinstripe socialist resigns as Austria's leader.
newsitem.headline: Pinstripe socialist resigns as Austria's leader.

text.p: Franz Vranitzky, who resigned as Austria's chancellor on Saturday after months of speculation over his future, made his mark as a statesman by acknowledging that Austria shared responsibility for the Nazi Holocaust.

Europe's second longest-serving government leader after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Vranitzky, 59, was Austria's most popular politician for most of his 10 1/2 years in power and did much to restore the country's image after the tarnished presidency of Kurt Waldheim.
A one-time national basketball player turned banker and politician, he cultivated the image of a cool-headed political manager with a steady hand on the government tiller.
He was a vote winner and for most of his tenure of power his Social Democrats were able to cash in on his popularity to cling on to their position as the country's biggest political party.

Vranitzky took over the Austrian government in June 1986 and his career has been shadowed by that of far right leader Joerg Haider, who was elected to head the nationalist Freedom Party the same year.

The writing appeared to be on the wall for Vranitzky after his party's disastrous results in last October's European elections -- the worst since its forebear, the Socialist Party, was founded after World War One.
"Dead Man Walking" is how the Vienna news magazine Profil described him the week after the Euro-poll.

Although visibly tired and clearly disappointed, Vranitzky told the political obituary writers to put away their pens as he would remain in office until Austria's next scheduled general elections in 1999. Few believed he would stay the course.

Assailed by critics gnawing away at his authority within his own party, he also had to contend with an increasingly fractious coalition partner, the conservative People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schussel.
A bitter struggle between the two parties over the privatisation of Creditanstalt, Austria's second biggest bank, may have tipped the balance and led Vranitzky to call it a day.
The decision to sell the bank to Bank Austria, indirectly controlled by the Social Democrats, was clinched only after a crisis meeting of the coalition parties last weekend.

Outside Austria, Vranitzky may be best remembered for doing what no other Austrian chancellor had done before -- he paid an official visit to Israel in 1991 and said Austria too had been responsible for the horrors committed by Hitler's Nazi regime.
He finally nailed the axiom that Austria was the first victim of Nazi aggression, saying many Austrians, not all, were willing accomplices in Nazi aggression.

His visit came in the last year of the presidency of Waldheim, a former United Nations secretary-general, who came under attack for his wartime record in Hitler's Wehrmacht and is still barred from entering the United States.
One of Vranitzky's most triumphant moments came in June 1994 when more than two-thirds of the Austrian electorate voted in a referendum to join the European Union.
Vranitzky, born into a working class family on October 4, 1937, was educated at the Vienna College of Commerce and after a period in industry joined the Austrian National Bank.

He was deputy head of Creditanstalt from 1976 to 1981 and chief of the country's then second biggest bank, Laenderbank, from 1981 to 1984. His banking career led one editor to dub him the "pin-striped socialist".
Vranitzky, married with a son and daughter, had little spare time for his hobbies of reading, tennis and hiking over the past two years as he struggled to keep his government in one piece.

The urbane, soft-spoken politician was given credit for Austria's economic upswing during his first four years in office. But the economic picture began to turn sour as the government grappled with an enormous budget deficit in 1995.
The coalition argued and then collapsed, forcing a snap election in December. The Social Democrats did better than expected after raising the spectre of Haider coming to power.

The euphoria was short-lived and the party won only a few thousand more votes than the far right in October's Euro-poll. Pollsters said half of the traditional Social Democrat working class vote had gone to the far right.

Vranitzky denied the dismal European results had anything to do with his resignation. He did not mention the constant bickering with Schuessel and the conservatives. But it was clear both had worn him down.
What he said as a parting shot was: "I have done my job. I've given my all."
